articles.title: A Utah restoration project treated 3,873 acres by thinning forests, removing juniper and repairing wetlands; during a 33,000-acre wildfire, earlier treated areas helped slow its spread
articles.summary: US News: Along Utah’s scenic Mirror Lake Highway, a large restoration project is showing why forest management is about more than planting trees or clearing br.
articles.body: Along Utah’s scenic Mirror Lake Highway, a large restoration project is showing why forest management is about more than planting trees or clearing brush. The recently completed Upper Provo Stewardship Project treated 3,873 acres across the Upper Provo Watershed, combining juniper removal, conifer thinning, hazard tree work, aspen enhancement and wetland restoration. The value of that preparation became clear during the 2024 Yellow Lake Fire, which burned more than 33,000 acres across the surrounding landscape. When the fire reached areas treated earlier, including parts of Iron Mine Mountain, officials reported that fire behaviour changed and existing fuel breaks helped slow the blaze. As described by the National Wild Turkey Federation, the project offers a real world example of how coordinated restoration can improve wildlife habitat, protect water and give firefighters a better chance to manage wildfire safely.A landscape with many needsThe Upper Provo Watershed is part of the Uinta Wasatch Cache National Forest, a region known for mountain forests, lakes, wetlands and recreation. The area supports wildlife, provides water and attracts people who hike, camp, fish and hunt.However, forests can become less resilient when vegetation grows too densely or when species expand into habitats where they were previously limited. Invasive juniper can take over grasslands, shrublands and young trees, reducing plant diversity and altering the availability of forage to wildlife. Dense conifer stands can also create continuous fuels for wildfires, allowing flames to move quickly through the canopy and understory.The restoration project was designed to address several problems at once. Instead of treating the landscape as a single uniform forest, partners used different methods in different places. Some areas needed juniper removal, while others required thinning, hazard tree work or wetland repair.That landscape scale approach recognises that forests, water and wildlife are connected. A healthier watershed can provide better habitat, reduce fire risk and improve the quality of water available to people and animals.What the restoration involvedThe Upper Provo project treated 3,873 acres through a partnership involving the National Wild Turkey Federation, the USDA Forest Service and Utah’s Watershed Restoration Initiative.The work included mastication of encroaching juniper. Mastication uses specialised machinery to cut and break woody vegetation into smaller pieces, reducing dense stands and returning material to the soil. It can open space for grasses, shrubs and other plants while reducing the amount of continuous fuel available to fire.Crews also thinned conifers and removed hazard trees. Thinning also creates a more diverse forest structure, and removing hazard trees improves safety around roads, recreation areas and work sites. A forest with a mix of tree spacing and tree ages may be more resilient than a forest with dense and even-aged tree stands.Aspen enhancement formed another part of the project. Aspen is an important component of western forests, providing for wildlife and diversity in landscapes dominated by conifers. Encouraging aspen regeneration can improve a wider range of vegetation and therefore habitat quality.Wetland restoration completed the picture. Wetlands hold water, filter sediment and nutrients, and provide habitat for wildlife. They can also prevent landscapes from drying out, creating natural breaks in otherwise continuous vegetation.The test came with the Yellow Lake FireThe restoration work faced a real world test during the 2024 Yellow Lake Fire. The wildfire burned more than 33,000 acres across the surrounding landscape, making it one of the largest recent fires in the region.As the fire reached previously treated areas, including treatments on Iron Mine Mountain, Forest Service officials reported that fire behaviour changed and existing fuel breaks helped slow the fire’s progression. That gave firefighters a better opportunity to manage the blaze and work more safely.A treatment does not make a forest fireproof. Flames can still enter thinned areas, especially during extreme weather with strong winds, low humidity and dry fuels. The goal is to change the fire’s intensity and speed, not to eliminate fire completely.When fuel loads are reduced, firefighters may have more choices. They can use roads, breaks and treated areas as locations to stage operations or attempt to contain the fire. Lower intensity flames may also give crews more time to respond before the fire reaches communities, infrastructure or especially valuable habitat.The Yellow Lake Fire provided evidence that restoration can influence fire behaviour under difficult conditions.Why fuel breaks matterA fuel break is an area where vegetation has been reduced or modified to slow the spread of fire. It may include thinned forest, treated grassland, a road corridor or a strip of land managed with prescribed fire.Fuel breaks are most effective when they are placed strategically and connected to other features. A single isolated treatment may have limited value if flames can simply move around it. Networks of treated areas can create more options for fire managers.The Upper Provo project was part of a wider effort to improve forest and watershed health across the region. Earlier treatments on the landscape contributed to the fuel breaks that influenced the Yellow Lake Fire.Such projects require planning because managers must balance fuel reduction with wildlife needs, soil protection and recreational access. Removing too much vegetation can cause erosion or reduce habitat, while leaving dense fuels untreated may allow severe fires to spread rapidly.The goal is a forest that can withstand disturbance without losing its essential functions.Benefits for wild turkeys and other wildlifeThe National Wild Turkey Federation supported the Upper Provo work because forest restoration can improve habitat for wild turkeys and many other species. Turkeys benefit from a mixture of forest cover, open areas, young vegetation and reliable water sources.A dense forest may provide shelter but limited food. Thinning and creating early successional vegetation can encourage grasses, forbs, shrubs and insects that serve as food for birds and other animals. Different vegetation layers also provide nesting, brooding and hiding areas.The benefits extend well beyond wild turkeys. Deer, elk, songbirds, pollinators and small mammals can use the varied habitats created by restoration. Aspen stands provide different food and shelter from conifer forests, while wetlands support amphibians, waterfowl and aquatic organisms.A mosaic of habitats is often more valuable than a landscape dominated by one vegetation type. Restoration can increase that variety while helping forests recover from past disturbance.Wetlands as natural infrastructureWetlands are sometimes overlooked because they occupy relatively small areas compared with forests and meadows. Their ecological importance is much larger than their size suggests.Wetlands slow water, trap sediment and filter pollutants before they reach streams and rivers. Their soils can store substantial amounts of water, helping maintain moisture during dry periods. They also provide breeding and feeding habitat for many species.Restoring wetlands within the Upper Provo Watershed supports both wildlife and people. Healthy wetland systems can improve water quality and contribute to more reliable flows downstream. They can also reduce the speed at which stormwater moves across the landscape, lowering erosion risks.Wetland restoration may involve reconnecting water to natural channels, improving vegetation, reducing disturbance or repairing areas damaged by roads and grazing. Each site requires a different approach, but the goal is to restore the wetland’s ability to hold and filter water.In a region facing drought, wildfire and changing precipitation patterns, that capacity is increasingly valuable.A partnership across boundariesThe Upper Provo project illustrates the value of collaboration. The watershed includes public land and resources that serve a wide range of users, but no single organisation has all the money, equipment and expertise required for landscape scale restoration.The Utah Watershed Restoration Initiative brings together state and federal agencies, sportsmen’s groups and other partners to identify priority projects. In 2026, the initiative allocated $6,491,866 for habitat projects, with the National Wild Turkey Federation contributing $223,200 toward 29 improvement projects and additional capacity for the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources.This structure allows organisations to share costs and coordinate work. A wildlife group may understand habitat needs, the Forest Service may manage the land and state agencies may provide technical expertise or funding. Together, they can accomplish more than any one partner working independently.The collaboration also helps connect different conservation goals. A project initially motivated by wildlife habitat can improve water quality and reduce wildfire risk. A fuels treatment can also enhance recreation and support forest regeneration.Restoration is an ongoing processCompleting 3,873 acres does not mean the Upper Provo Watershed will never need additional work. Forests continue to grow, juniper can return and wildfire conditions change. Wetlands require monitoring to ensure that restored water flows and vegetation remain healthy.Managers will need to observe how wildlife responds, whether aspen regeneration succeeds and whether treated areas maintain their ability to influence fire behaviour. Future treatments may be required to maintain fuel breaks or expand restoration into connected areas.The lessons from the Yellow Lake Fire can help guide that work. Fire managers can study where flames slowed, where they intensified and how different treatments performed under the same weather conditions. This information improves the design of future projects.Long term conservation depends on that feedback. Restoration is most effective when managers treat each project as part of a continuing cycle of action, monitoring and adjustment.A practical example of resilienceThe Upper Provo Stewardship Project demonstrates what resilience looks like on the ground. It does not promise to prevent every wildfire or solve every habitat problem. Instead, it changes the landscape so forests, wetlands and communities have a better chance of absorbing disturbance.The 2024 Yellow Lake Fire showed that the effort had practical value. They didn’t put the fire out in the treated areas, but they helped change the behaviour of the fire and gave firefighters more options. That outcome supports continued investment in forest management and watershed restoration.The project also shows that conservation benefits rarely exist in isolation. Thinning can support wildlife and reduce fuels. Wetland work can improve water and habitat. Aspen enhancement can add diversity and help forests recover.Across 3,873 acres, the Upper Provo landscape received more than a single treatment. It received a coordinated effort to make the watershed healthier, safer and more capable of supporting life.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: By 2022, British communities had adopted more than 7,000 phone boxes for £1 each and turned them into libraries, book exchanges and defibrillator stations
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how British communities are giving a new lease of life to obsolete phone boxes by converting them into libraries, cafés, and lifesaving defibrillators, reviving a piece of history.
articles.body: Britain’s famous telephone boxes were an essential part of everyday life for much of the 20th century. These boxes offered a way to make a call from anywhere, including the street corner, village green or railway station at a time when most people did not carry a mobile phone in their pockets. However, the rapid spread of mobile phones soon eroded the telephone boxes’ original purpose. By the 2020s, thousands of the boxes were rarely used.Instead of simply removing them, British communities have adopted more than 7,000 phone boxes since 2008 for £1 each through BT’s Adopt a Kiosk scheme, according to The Guardian in April 2022. The former telephone boxes were turned into miniature libraries and art galleries. Meanwhile, others were repurposed to house publicly accessible defibrillators.How a £1 initiative gave redundant telephone booths a second lifeIn 2008, to take over redundant red telephone boxes instead of having them removed, BT launched Adopt a Kiosk. The scheme allowed recognised public bodies like town, parish and community councils, including registered charities, to acquire qualifying kiosks for £1. Under these terms, the internal telecommunications machinery is completely decommissioned and uninstalled prior to the community taking physical possession of the shell for repurposing. This innovative idea soon produced some small community facilities. BT reported that two former red boxes were acquired by Appleton Parish Council in Cheshire and were converted into different public amenities. One box became a book exchange, while the other was fitted out to house a defibrillator.Other adopted kiosks soon found other functions as well. Communities reportedly found uses that allowed the structures to remain a part of their local landscape despite losing their original telecommunications function. By 2021, records reported that more than 6,600 phone boxes had already been adopted through the scheme, with The Guardian saying that by 2022, the said figure had passed 7,000, thus making the £1 scheme a nationwide reuse programme instead of a collection of isolated village projects. As enclosed kiosks were well suited to provide a recognisable, publicly accessible location for emergency calls, defibrillators became one of the most practical conversions.Under this scheme, not all phone boxes were transformedJust because there was a decline in ordinary use, it did not necessarily mean that every remaining payphone was obsolete. Ofcom’s evidence showed that public call boxes continued to play a role in regions where people lacked a working mobile phone or where mobile coverage was poor. At the time of The Guardian’s report in 2022, around 5 million calls were still being made from British phone boxes each year. Ofcom’s data suggests that between May 2019 and May 2020, approximately 150,000 calls were made to emergency services. This included about 25,000 calls to Childline and 20,000 to Samaritans.The regulator introduced stronger guidelines in June 2022, preventing BT and KCOM from removing certain boxes when they were still needed in the communities. A box could qualify for protection if, among other conditions, it was in a region without coverage from all four mobile networks, had recorded at least 52 calls over the past 12 months, was in an area with a high frequency of accidents or suicides, or if there was any other evidence that it was reasonably needed, such as use for helplines or local emergency services.A British landmark became a part of community infrastructureThe famous red kiosks had become a part of the country’s visual landscape long before mobile phones appeared. Government guidance on former telephone kiosks notes that the red designs included the K2, introduced following Giles Gilbert Scott’s 1924 design, and the later K6, of which around 60,000 were installed. The 2008 scheme allowed the phone boxes to retain their recognisable red legacy while its interior was given an entirely different function.Looking ahead to subsequent project expansions, BT’s 2023 report said that more than 7,200 phone boxes had been adopted by communities across the UK since 2008, while around 20,000 working payphones remained, including about 3,000 in traditional red kiosks. This legacy infrastructure network now continues to serve as an enduring, adaptive model for local civic engagement and architectural preservation.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: How Trump's EV rollback is hitting America's auto-factory revival
articles.summary: US News: America’s electric vehicle manufacturing revival is losing momentum as billions of dollars in planned EV and battery investments are cancelled, delaye.
articles.body: America’s electric vehicle manufacturing revival is losing momentum as billions of dollars in planned EV and battery investments are cancelled, delayed or scaled back amid weaker demand and President Donald Trump’s rollback of policies that supported the industry.A Reuters investigation found that nearly $20 billion in EV-related projects were cancelled in 2025, while new investment announcements fell to about $6.5 billion from a peak of $55 billion in 2023. The cancelled projects had represented around 27,000 promised jobs, according to Reuters’ analysis of Atlas Public Policy data.The impact is visible at Lordstown, Ohio, where a $2.3 billion battery plant halted production in January. About 480 workers were indefinitely laid off, while another 850 were told they would not be needed for months.The reversal is notable because much of the earlier investment went to Republican-leaning states. Reuters found that 87 percent of announced EV-related investment was in states won by Trump in 2024, while about 80 percent of cancelled projects were in those states.The slowdown comes as the US EV market was already facing weaker-than-expected demand. Automakers had scaled up production and battery capacity based on forecasts of rapid EV adoption, but sales failed to grow at the expected pace, forcing companies to rethink investment plans.Trump’s decision to end the $7,500 federal EV tax credit added another setback. The credit had helped lower the upfront cost of electric vehicles, but its removal weakened an important incentive for buyers as automakers were already cutting back on EV plans.The policy shift also affected companies that had expanded in anticipation of sustained government support. Ford, for instance, has moved to repurpose part of its planned EV manufacturing capacity for gasoline-powered vehicles, reflecting the changing economics of the US auto market.Trump’s broader push to roll back Biden-era EV policies has added uncertainty for automakers and battery manufacturers. The administration has argued that the earlier incentives distorted the market by pushing consumers towards electric vehicles, while its policy now gives greater room for gasoline-powered cars and trucks.Tariffs have also raised costs for some battery materials and components, while tighter immigration policies have complicated efforts by companies to bring specialised engineers and technicians to new US plants.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: Middle East News: Saudi Arabia's air defences intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone just south of Mecca on Tuesday before it could enter the holy city's restricted a.
articles.body: Saudi Arabia's air defences intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone just south of Mecca on Tuesday before it could enter the holy city's restricted airspace.Saudi military spokesperson Turki al-Malki described the security of the holy sites and pilgrims as a “red line” and warned of measures against the Houthis.However,Houthi spokesperson Hazem al-Assad rejected it, writing on X: “The claims about targeting Mecca are a worn-out lie that has been used before and no longer fools anyone.”Why it matters: Mecca changes the political stakesMecca is the destination of the Haj and home to the Kaaba, towards which Muslims worldwide pray. Saudi Arabia’s responsibility for the holy sites is central to the monarchy’s standing across the Muslim world.A strike on or near Mecca could carry consequences that military and economic calculations cannot easily contain.For Riyadh, that creates a particularly difficult test. It must demonstrate that it can protect the sites while avoiding an escalation that could expose them to further danger.Even an accidental strike could generate public anger for retaliation.It could also widen the diplomatic stakes. Governments that have tried to maintain distance from the fighting could face calls to support the protection of the holy sites.But that would not automatically produce a military coalition. Condemning a threat to Mecca and committing forces to fight against Houthis are very different decisions.For India, the concern would extend beyond oil prices to pilgrims, Indian nationals in Saudi Arabia and relations with a major Gulf partner.Zoom in: The ‘Gate of Tears’ closes inBab el-Mandeb, also known as the ‘Gate of Tears’, connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean. For ships using the Suez route between Europe and Asia, it is an essential passage.Houthi fighters have captured Mokha and Dhabab on Yemen’s coast and took Perim Island, which divides the strait into two shipping channels.Those gains strengthen their capacity to threaten vessels.For Saudi Arabia, the geography is unforgiving:To the east, Iranian attacks have made the Strait of Hormuz hazardous.Across the kingdom, the East-West Pipeline provided a way to move crude towards the Red Sea.To the southwest, Houthi advances threaten the onward route towards Saudi Arabia’s Asian customers.Red Sea exports can also travel north through the Suez Canal or Egyptian pipeline infrastructure. Bab el-Mandeb is therefore not the exit for every Saudi shipment. But disrupting the southern passage makes access to Asian markets harder.Now the pipeline itself has been hit. Bloomberg reported that British authorities feared it could remain largely shut for six weeks.Between the lines: MBS’s past meets his futureThe Houthis present a particularly uncomfortable challenge for the Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) because they connect his earliest major military gamble with his central economic ambition.MBS spearheaded Saudi Arabia’s intervention in Yemen in 2015. Years of fighting failed to dislodge the movement. Riyadh subsequently sought to reduce its involvement, with a 2022 truce bringing a period of relative calm.The renewed offensive threatens that effort to disengage.It also undermines the conditions needed for his economic transformation programme: predictable revenues, investor confidence, tourism and a reputation for stability.What next: Allies, escalation or another bargain?MBS asked Donald Trump for military help against Houthis but the US President did not agree for air strikes. He instead offered Riyadh support with intelligence sharing and targeting.Israel is already providing intelligence assistance to Saudi Arabia in its fight against Houthis, a Jerusalem Post report said on Tuesday.MBS visited Egypt on Tuesday to meet President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi. According to AP, the crown prince and Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi affirmed their commitment to maritime security. Neither government announced specific military steps, though.Egypt has its own reasons to want safer shipping: Red Sea disruption has reduced Suez Canal traffic and revenues. But shared economic interests do not guarantee Egyptian participation in another Yemen campaign.Analyst HA Hellyer told AP: “I don't think MBS wants troops from Cairo, which he knows would be a very difficult ask.”The bottom lineWill Saudi Arabia invoke the Mecca pact in case the holy place is attacked by the Houthis?Will Pakistan comes to the rescue of the Saudi Crown Prince?As of now, Pakistan has been ambivalent about its purported response.As of now, MBS is being tested on three fronts simultaneously: Oil, tourism and now the symbolic security of Mecca itself.For MBS, the challenge is to protect Mecca and keep oil without getting dragged into another long war.(With inputs from agencies)Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1980, a homeless salesman put his final $700 into shampoo he sold door to door; his company later reached $900 million in annual sales
articles.summary: US News: Discover how John Paul DeJoria transformed a mere $700 investment into a billion-dollar hair care empire with Paul Mitchell. Explore their entrepreneurial journey and the secrets behind their success!
articles.body: In 1980, John Paul DeJoria was living in an old Rolls-Royce and trying to make a living selling hair-care products. He had already worked a string of jobs, including selling encyclopaedias door to door, and had become accustomed to hearing no. His next gamble was different. Together with hairstylist Paul Mitchell, he put just $700 into a new professional hair-care business. The products were carried from salon to salon in the trunk of DeJoria’s car, with the founders relying on personal sales rather than a large advertising budget.According to Paul Mitchell’s official history, the idea was straightforward: create professional-quality hair products that hairdressers could use in their salons and recommend to their customers. The first range consisted of three products: Shampoo One, Shampoo Two and The Conditioner. The company began with $700 and those three products in 1980. The brand eventually grew into a global hair-care business with more than 100 products sold in more than 80 countries.The business grew through rejectionDeJoria's earlier experience selling encyclopaedias door to door proved useful when he started the hair-care business. The job had taught him how to approach strangers, handle rejection and keep going when a sale did not come easily. Those skills became important when he began introducing the new products to salon owners, many of whom had no reason to take a chance on an unfamiliar brand.The early months were far from glamorous. Stanford Graduate School of Business reported that DeJoria sold the products from the boot of his car and used his sales experience to approach salons directly. The company lost money during its first two years, and DeJoria recalled a period when he struggled to pay the bills. By 1982, however, the business had reached the point where it could pay what it owed on time.Instead of immediately trying to sell their products in supermarkets, they decided to target professional salons. The owners started networking with hairdressers who would promote and advise customers to buy them. According to the history of the company recorded by the US Tax Court, the first batch of the products was sold during a beauty show in 1980 for $10,000, and then the company started to distribute its product through professional channels. This helped the company establish its distinct identity. Paul Mitchell was marketed as a product developed for hairdressers, not just another shampoo competing for shelf space in stores.From $700 to a global brandResearch published in Global Business and Organisational Excellence examined necessity entrepreneurship and found that unemployment, financial pressure and limited economic opportunities can encourage people to start their own businesses. Having a reason to start is only the beginning. Whether such a business survives depends on how effectively the founders find customers, use limited resources and respond to challenges. For DeJoria and Mitchell, the business gradually gained momentum as salons began reordering their products. The range expanded, distribution widened, and the company continued to build its identity around professional hairdressers. When Paul Mitchell died of cancer in 1989, DeJoria carried on with the business and later expanded into other ventures, including Patrón tequila.The company's later scale was hard to imagine from those early days. Stanford Graduate School of Business reported that John Paul Mitchell Systems reached $900 million in sales in 2010, while Forbes later reported annual sales of around $900 million in 2019. The figures show how far the company had travelled from the $700 that DeJoria and Mitchell had pooled at the beginning.The company's simple approach helped it stand out in the market. DeJoria lacked the means of engaging in a large-scale advertising campaign and therefore went straight to the salons to persuade the hairdressers to use their products. In these initial conversations, the young company was able to secure its first customers and build a professional network through which it would grow its brand. A few bottles placed in the trunk of a car would later become an international hair-care business worth hundreds of millions of dollars annually.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: India-Pakistan naval ships collide in Arabian Sea: What 1991 pact says
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: India on Wednesday said the conduct of a Pakistani naval ship that led to a collision with an Indian Navy vessel in international waters wa.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India on Wednesday said the conduct of a Pakistani naval ship that led to a collision with an Indian Navy vessel in international waters was in direct contravention of Article 10 of a 1991 bilateral agreement between the two countries.India conveyed strong protest over the incident to Pakistan's Charge d'Affaires.“The Charge d'Affaires of the High Commission for the Islamic Republic of Pakistan in New Delhi was summoned to the ministry of external affairs today and a strong protest was lodged with him over the unacceptable and unprofessional conduct of Pakistani naval units at sea that led to a collision with a unit of the Indian Navy,” the ministry said in a statement."While the incident, which took place in international waters, did not cause any major damage, the conduct of the Pakistani naval ship was in direct contravention of Article 10 of the Agreement between India and Pakistan on Advance Notice on Military Exercises, Manoeuvres and Troops Movements of April 1991," it added.The ministry further said that it advised the Pakistani diplomat "to convey to the concerned Pakistani authorities the need for all military units to observe due care and respect the provisions of the relevant agreements between the two sides in order to prevent any repeat of such incidents.""The Charge d'Affaires of India in Islamabad has also been instructed to lodge a similar protest with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan," it said.According to agency sources, a Pakistani naval ship came close to a frontline Indian Navy warship during a routine surveillance mission in the North Arabian Sea."The Pakistani vessel was travelling at high speed and manoeuvring in an “unprofessional and unsafe manner,” ANI reported quoting sources.India-Pakistan 1991 pact: What does it sayThe pact between Islamabad and Delhi was signed in April 1991 as part of a series of confidence-building measures between both countries. The measures were aimed at fostering trust and preventing accidental or unintended military confrontations.Under the agreement, the land, naval and air forces of both countries are to avoid major exercises close to each other. If such exercises are conducted within specified areas, the main force cannot be directed towards the other side and there should be no logistical build-up close to it.Under this pact, both nations agreed to provide notification to each other about significant military exercises, manoeuvres and troop movements near the border."Their Land, Naval and Air Forces will avoid holding major military manoeuvres and exercises in close proximity to each other. However if such exercises are held within distances as prescribed in this Agreement, the strategic direction of the main force being exercised will not be towards the other side, nor will any logistics build up be carried out close to it," the agreement says.Article 10 of the agreement says that naval ships and submarines of both countries have to maintain a distance of three Nautical Miles from each other."The Naval ships and submarines belonging to the other country are not to close less than three Nautical Miles (NMs) from each other so as to avoid any accident while operating in international waters," it says.Along with the 1991 agreement, New Delhi and Islamabad also committed themselves under the Memorandum of Understanding signed at Lahore on February 21, 1999, to conclude a “Prevention of Incidents at Sea” agreement to ensure the safety of navigation by their naval vessels and aircraft.The provision formed part of the Lahore confidence-building process and reflected the two countries’ intention to establish arrangements to prevent accidents and dangerous encounters at sea.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Video: Cabin panels fall, passengers scream as Iran Boeing 737 makes emergency landing
articles.summary: Middle East News: A Sepehran Airlines Boeing 737 flying from Mashhad to Kermanshah in Iran was forced to return to Mashhad shortly after takeoff after a tyre problem an.
articles.body: A Sepehran Airlines Boeing 737 flying from Mashhad to Kermanshah in Iran was forced to return to Mashhad shortly after takeoff after a tyre problem and a reported engine emergency, with dramatic cabin footage showing interior panels coming loose during severe shaking.According to Aviation Today, the aircraft developed the problem after leaving Mashhad airport on September 15. Iran’s Razavi Khorasan provincial airports authority said the outer tread had separated from one of the aircraft’s tyres as it departed the runway. Officials clarified that the tyre itself had not burst.The pilot subsequently reported an engine emergency to air traffic control and requested permission to return to Mashhad. The aircraft landed safely, and no injuries were reported among those on board.Videos from inside the aircraft showed passengers reacting in panic as the Boeing 737 experienced intense shaking. Sections of the cabin’s overhead lining and interior panels appeared to detach and fall, while passengers could be heard screaming. Some belongings also fell from overhead compartments.The footage does not indicate that the aircraft’s main fuselage or structural roof collapsed. The visible damage appears to involve cabin interior panels and lining.The exact relationship between the tyre problem and the reported engine emergency remains unclear. Iranian aviation authorities are investigating the incident, and there is currently no confirmed finding that the tyre problem caused damage to the engine.The incident comes amid wider scrutiny of Iran’s ageing commercial aircraft fleet, which has faced long-standing difficulties in accessing Western aircraft, spare parts and maintenance support because of international sanctions.Sepehran Airlines has also experienced another Boeing 737 incident at Mashhad in recent weeks. On August 25, a Boeing 737-500 reportedly veered off the runway after landing, with its nose landing gear collapsing. No injuries were reported in that incident.Authorities are expected to examine the aircraft’s tyre, landing gear, engines and cabin systems to establish what triggered the latest emergency and why the cabin interior was damaged during the flight.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Don Butler moved to his family's New York farm at 7, when its 1887 barn was still the primary barn; decades later, 75 acres are permanently protected amid weekly solar-farm solicitations
articles.summary: US News: When Don Butler moved to his family's farm in Northumberland, New York, at age 7, the property's large red barn, marked with 1887 on its slate roof, w.
articles.body: When Don Butler moved to his family's farm in Northumberland, New York, at age 7, the property's large red barn, marked with 1887 on its slate roof, was still the primary barn. Decades later, much has changed around the farm, from the decline of smaller dairy operations to growing pressure from development and solar projects. According to a report by WAMC Northeast Public Radio, 75 acres of the Butler Family Farm have now been placed under a conservation easement with Saratoga PLAN, permanently protecting the land for agricultural use. Butler and his family members told WAMC about the farm's history, the changes they have witnessed and why preserving the property has become increasingly important.A farm that has changed over generationsThe Butler Family Farm covers about 250 acres, but its agricultural operation looks very different from when Butler was growing up there. The farm was once a milking operation with around 60 dairy cattle. Today, the family has three beef heifers, while the property primarily produces dry hay for nearby cattle farms. Butler told WAMC that farming remains common in the area stretching from Gansevoort through Moreau, Northumberland and into Saratoga. What has changed, he said, is the number and size of farms. Smaller operations have increasingly been consolidated into larger ones. That shift has made it more difficult for smaller farms to remain viable, even though agriculture continues to be an important part of the landscape.The family's decision to protect 75 acres comes as development pressure continues to grow in Saratoga County. According to US Census Bureau, the county's population increased by 6.7% between 2015 and 2025.Solar proposals keep arrivingFor Butler, protecting the land is also connected to the growing interest in using farmland for other purposes. As he explained to WAMC, the family receives nearly weekly solicitations for solar farms, along with occasional approaches related to development. The 75-acre section is particularly attractive from a development perspective because it has substantial road frontage, including access along Stonebridge Road and another public road.Butler has made his position on the issue clear. He told WAMC that he does not believe productive farmland should be used for solar installations. The conservation easement provides a way to keep the protected portion of the property in agricultural use while removing the possibility of future development on those acres. Saratoga PLAN, the nonprofit involved in the agreement, has conserved more than 14,000 acres overall. With the Butler family's property, it says more than 540 acres have now been protected in Northumberland.What the easement means for the familyA conservation easement allows land to remain privately owned while placing permanent restrictions on certain future uses. In this case, the arrangement protects the 75 acres as farmland rather than allowing the property to be converted to another use. For Butler's daughter, Holly Rippon-Butler, the arrangement also has significance beyond her own family's property.Rippon-Butler is the farm's third-generation caretaker and works as an independent consultant with organisations that help farmers succeed and gain access to land. She told WAMC that conservation easements can help make farmland more affordable for farmers by reducing the value associated with its development potential. That can matter in areas where agricultural land is expensive because farmers are competing with buyers who have other plans for the property. As Rippon-Butler explained to WAMC, there can be a significant gap between what a farm business can generate and the amount of money required to purchase farmland near markets, with good soils and the infrastructure needed for agriculture. Removing development potential can help bring the price of land closer to what its agricultural use can support.Land with a long family historyThe decision to protect the property also carries a history that stretches back well before the latest conservation agreement. The now-protected land was considered as a possible location for a municipal dump in 1998, the same year Rippon-Butler was born. For her mother, Gwenne Rippon, protecting the property represents the continuation of an effort that began with earlier generations of the family. According to WAMC, Gwenne Rippon said she had watched Don Butler's parents make sacrifices to keep the farm operating and wanted to do what she could to ensure the land remained in farming. The conservation agreement now gives that goal a permanent framework.Keeping farmland in agricultureThe Butler family's decision reflects a wider challenge for agricultural communities located near growing population centres. As housing, commercial projects and renewable-energy proposals compete for land, working farms can face pressure from uses that may generate more value than agriculture alone. The conservation easement does not transfer the farm to public ownership. Instead, the family retains the land while limiting its future development potential. For Butler, that means the protected acreage can continue to form part of the family farm rather than becoming a subdivision or another non-agricultural project. For Rippon-Butler, it also demonstrates how conservation tools can potentially help younger farmers access land without having to compete with buyers interested in its development value. And for Rippon, it represents the outcome of a family effort to keep the property in farming.The 1887 barn that Butler remembers from childhood remains a marker of the farm's long history. While the operation itself has evolved from a 60-cow dairy to a smaller farm producing hay and raising a few beef cattle, 75 acres now have a permanently protected agricultural future, even as development and solar-farm proposals continue to reach farms across the growing Saratoga County region.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Calvin Klein’s former 1894 East Hampton estate sold for $85 million in 2021; after a major renovation, the 8.22-acre compound is now asking $165 million
articles.summary: US News: For a property that has already changed hands for tens of millions of dollars, this East Hampton estate is making an even bigger play the second time .
articles.body: For a property that has already changed hands for tens of millions of dollars, this East Hampton estate is making an even bigger play the second time around. Once owned by Calvin Klein, the sprawling oceanfront compound returned to the market in the month of June with a $165 million price tag, putting it within striking distance of the Hamptons’ long-standing residential sales record. Scroll down to read the story of its trajectory.A storied East Hampton addressMore than a decade ago, hedge fund manager Barry Rosenstein set the benchmark for East Hampton real estate when he paid $147 million for an 18-acre property. That record has held ever since, but the latest listing could put it under pressure.According to a report by ELLE Decor, Klein sold his own East Hampton estate in 2021 in an off-market transaction reportedly valued at $85 million. The fashion designer had owned the property since 1987, when he purchased the roughly 8,900-square-foot home with his then-wife, Kelly Rector.The estate had already enjoyed a notable pedigree. Klein and Rector acquired it from the family of Juan Trippe, the former president of Pan American World Airways, and later brought in renowned architect Thierry Despont for an extensive renovation.A 19th-century home with modern flairOriginally built in the 1890s, the main residence was designed by Joseph Greenleaf Thorp, the architect behind the famous Grey Gardens property. The Shingle Style home retains many of the period details that give it its character, including beamed ceilings, wide-plank floors, wainscoting and crown molding.Those traditional elements sit alongside decidedly contemporary touches. Inside, a mirrored catwalk stretches across the living room, while a dramatic two-story fireplace creates a striking focal point.The property also expanded beyond the main house during Klein’s ownership. A pool was added to the grounds, along with a boathouse on Georgica Pond. The boathouse is reportedly the only working one on the coastal lagoon.A major new renovationAs per the ELLE Deco report, the current owner has undertaken another significant round of improvements, bringing the historic estate up to modern standards without stripping away its old-world appeal.Updates include impact-resistant windows and doors, energy-efficient heating and cooling systems, smart-home technology and advanced security. The result is a property that combines the architectural character of a centuries-old East Hampton retreat with the infrastructure expected of a contemporary luxury compound.Outside, the amenities are equally substantial. A red-clay tennis court, expansive entertaining spaces and 500 feet of ocean frontage give the estate an unmistakably resort-like feel.Room to build even morePerhaps one of the most significant details is the property's development potential. The 8.22-acre compound can be divided into two parcels, with one parcel carrying its own building rights for an additional residence.That flexibility adds another layer of appeal to an already rare offering. Between its ocean frontage, architectural history, celebrity provenance and substantial acreage, the former Calvin Klein estate is now positioned as one of the most closely watched luxury listings in East Hampton.Images Courtesy: InstagramCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: No drones, metal detectors: Family of slain US activist Charlie Kirk accuses Utah varsity of 'stunning' security lapses
articles.summary: US News: The family of slain US conservative activist Charlie Kirk has accused Utah Valley University (UVU) and state officials of a series of security failure.
articles.body: The family of slain US conservative activist Charlie Kirk has accused Utah Valley University (UVU) and state officials of a series of security failures that allegedly left him exposed to a rooftop gunman before he was fatally shot at a campus event in September 2025.The allegations were made in a legal notice filed on September 9, a mandatory step under Utah law before Kirk’s heirs can bring a wrongful-death claim against public entities. The notice names the university, its then-president Astrid Tuminez, the campus police department and its chief, Jeffrey Long, as well as the state of Utah.Kirk, 31, was addressing students at an outdoor debate at the university’s campus in Orem on September 10, 2025, when a gunman fired from a rooftop more than 400 feet (122 metres) away, according to the notice.Attorneys for Kirk’s family said his death followed a series of “reckless decisions” by university officials.“The risk of a rooftop shooter should have been especially top-of-mind given the attempted assassination of President Trump, Charlie Kirk’s close friend and political ally, by a rooftop shooter the previous year,” family attorney D. Loren Washburn wrote in the notice.A review by news agency AP found that the campus police presence was below recommended levels for a university of its size. Authorities also did not deploy a drone to monitor rooftops or coordinate with local law enforcement to secure the event, which drew about 3,000 people. There were no bag checks or metal detectors.The family further alleged that officials failed to carry out an adequate risk assessment, establish a secure perimeter or ensure that first responders were immediately available.“Tragically, the UVU Parties took none of these safety measures — steps only they had the authority to take — resulting in a situation that rendered Mr. Kirk helpless before his assassin,” Washburn wrote.The notice also alleges that Kirk was taken to a nearby hospital in a private vehicle rather than an ambulance after he was shot.Long said after the shooting that six campus officers had staffed the event and coordinated with Kirk’s eight-person private security team. The university later said it was expanding its police force.The allegations come as the criminal case against Tyler Robinson, 23, proceeds towards trial. Prosecutors accuse him of killing Kirk and have charged him with seven offences, including aggravated murder, which is punishable by death in Utah.During a preliminary hearing, Utah County prosecutor Ryan McBride presented surveillance footage that he said showed Robinson taking up a position before the shooting.“He lay down in a prone position, and he would have seen this mass of people of 3,000-plus people there for the event, took aim, put his crosshairs on Charlie Kirk and fired,” McBride told the court.Defence lawyer Staci Visser disputed the prosecution’s account, arguing that the shooting endangered no one but Kirk. Prosecutors have also cited DNA evidence they say links Robinson to a rifle found near the scene and a handwritten note allegedly left for his romantic partner: “I had the opportunity to take out Charlie Kirk, and I took it.”A judge has ordered the case to proceed towards trial. Robinson has not yet entered a plea, and no trial date has been set.The university has been asked for comment on the family’s allegations, while the Utah Attorney General’s Office said it does not comment on potential litigation.The notice does not specify the damages the family may seek, leaving the possible civil claim and the university’s response as the next significant developments.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Quote of the day by Plato: "The first and best victory is to conquer self. To be conquered by self is..."
articles.summary: Europe News: Two people can face down a difficult external challenge and describe their success in very different terms. One credits the win entirely to overcoming.
articles.body: Two people can face down a difficult external challenge and describe their success in very different terms. One credits the win entirely to overcoming an opponent, a competitor, a rival, treating victory as something that happens strictly between two separate, opposing parties. The other recognises that the harder, more decisive battle actually happened somewhere else entirely, inside their own impulses, fears, and appetites, long before the external contest was ever properly settled. Plato, in the Laws, one of his final dialogues, ranked these two kinds of victory explicitly and without much hedging, placing self-mastery firmly above any triumph over an external opponent, and treating defeat by one's own worse impulses as a genuinely deeper, more shameful failure than any loss to an outside rival could ever really be.Quote of the day by Plato"The first and best victory is to conquer self. To be conquered by self is, of all things, the most shameful and vile."Written in Plato's most practical, least idealised dialogueWhat gives this line particular weight is where it appears. Unlike the more famous Republic, which sketches an idealised philosophical city ruled by philosopher-kings, the Laws is widely considered Plato's most concrete, practically minded work, written in his old age and focused on the detailed legal and social structures a real, workable city would actually need. Self-mastery, in that context, wasn't presented as an abstract virtue for philosophers alone to pursue. It was treated as a foundational requirement for any citizen expected to participate responsibly in a functioning community, since a person unable to govern their own impulses could hardly be trusted to help govern anyone else's affairs, or even their own household, well.That emphasis reflects a theme running through much of Plato's broader philosophy, inherited in part from his teacher Socrates, who was famous for arguing that genuine wisdom began with confronting one's own ignorance and impulses honestly rather than assuming external achievements were the real measure of a well-lived life. Placing self-conquest above conquest of others wasn't simply a moral flourish for Plato. It reflected a considered view about where the actual difficulty, and the actual value, of virtue was located, inside the person doing the striving rather than in whatever external contest they happened to be measured against.A simple way to actually use this ideaThe useful move here is noticing how much of a difficult situation is actually an external problem, and how much is really a struggle with one's own impatience, fear, or appetite, dressed up convincingly as an external problem so it's easier to blame something outside yourself. It's often much easier to focus entirely on an outside obstacle, a rival, a deadline, a difficult circumstance, than to admit that the harder, less flattering part of the struggle is actually internal, and that no amount of managing the external situation will resolve it on its own.A fair test, in the middle of any difficult contest or decision, is to ask honestly which part of the struggle is actually external, and which part is really about managing your own impulses well enough to handle the external part effectively at all. That question won't make the external challenge disappear. It usually reveals which battle actually needs to be won first, and makes it much harder to keep quietly losing the internal one while insisting the real fight is happening somewhere else entirely.Other quotes from Plato's Laws"Education certainly gives victory, although victory sometimes produces forgetfulness of education." "Self-love is the source of that ignorant conceit of knowledge which is always doing and never succeeding." "There is simple ignorance, which is the source of lighter offences, and double ignorance, which is accompanied by a conceit of wisdom."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'It is defensive, nothing aggressive': Pak scrambles to define Mecca pact after Houthi attack
articles.summary: Pakistan News: Pakistan’s military has rushed to give a definition to the newly formed Mecca Defence Alliance, saying the pact with Saudi Arabia and Turkey is meant .
articles.body: Pakistan’s military has rushed to give a definition to the newly formed Mecca Defence Alliance, saying the pact with Saudi Arabia and Turkey is meant for collective deterrence and has “no regional aspirations”, even as questions grow over how the agreement would work if one of its members comes under attack.Pakistan’s inter-services public relations (ISPR) director general Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, speaking to Al Arabiya, said the agreement was “defensive” and “complementary” to the three countries’ existing alliances and relationships.“It is defensive. There’s nothing aggressive. There are no regional aspirations. It is collective deterrence,” Chaudhry said.The comments come as the pact faces questions over its first potential test. The alliance has been put under scrutiny amid the conflict involving Saudi Arabia and Houthi forces, with uncertainty over whether Riyadh has sought military assistance from Islamabad and how Pakistan would respond if it did.The pact was signed on August 7 and says an attack on one member would be treated as an attack on all. Pakistan is to initially head its secretariat for three years.Also read: Mecca Pact, but no troops yet: Pakistan expresses 'solidarity' with Saudi Arabia after Houthi attacks on kingdomWhat happens if Saudi Arabia is attacked?Chaudhry was pressed on precisely that question during the Al Arabiya interview: whether Pakistan had a mutual defence obligation under the agreement and what it would actually do if one of the members came under attack.He said the publicly released text made the mutual defence commitment clear, but stressed that the operational details of how such a commitment would be implemented were classified.“What you’re asking is the how part — how we are going to defend Pakistan against any aggression,” he said, adding that such decisions would be for the three countries to make.The distinction is significant because the pact has not yet been tested in an actual conflict. The first major test could become the escalating Houthi-Saudi confrontation, with questions remaining over when an attack would trigger the alliance and what form military assistance would take.The uncertainty is also not entirely new. Pakistan’s parliament had unanimously rejected a request in 2015 to send troops to join the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis. Pakistan also shares a long border with Iran, giving Islamabad an additional security consideration as it navigates its relationship with Riyadh and Tehran.Not a Muslim military blocChaudhry also rejected the idea that the Mecca Defence Alliance was being designed as a broader Muslim military bloc.“There is nothing in the pact that says that it is a Muslim alliance,” he said, describing it instead as an arrangement aimed at regional stability.He said other countries could potentially join if they shared the principles of non-aggression, non-interference and collective deterrence, but stressed that any expansion would be a decision for the leaders of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey.The comments come amid speculation about possible expansion of the grouping. Turkey had previously suggested Egypt could join, although Cairo has not confirmed any such move. Pakistan’s foreign office has meanwhile said the immediate priority was to consolidate the new organisation before considering expansion.Pakistan says pact does not compete with China tiesChaudhry also sought to reassure Beijing that the new arrangement was not aimed at competing with Pakistan’s relationship with China.Asked whether the alliance complemented or competed with Islamabad’s ties with Beijing, he said it was complementary.He argued that Pakistan’s relationships with Saudi Arabia and Turkey were longstanding and that the three countries also maintained good relations with China.“Everyone understands that this is defensive,” Chaudhry said, adding that the pact was intended to maintain “stability and peace in the region”.Why Pakistan is walking a diplomatic tightropeThe military spokesperson was also asked whether the defence pact complicated Pakistan’s efforts to mediate between the US and Iran amid the ongoing Middle East conflict.Chaudhry rejected that suggestion, saying the pact formalised longstanding relationships rather than creating a new strategic alignment against another country.He described Pakistan as being in a “unique position” because of its engagement with different countries and said Islamabad could therefore act as an “objective arbiter of peace” and an “honest broker”.Pakistan, he said, wanted a negotiated and peaceful resolution rather than a military solution.That position is particularly relevant as Islamabad balances its strategic relationship with Saudi Arabia with its geographic proximity to Iran.Chaudhry said Pakistan's decision to mediate was driven by a desire for regional peace and that the country would continue engaging the parties involved.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Union home minister Amit Shah on Wednesday said the Centre has declared the Pakistan-based Shahzad Bhatti Network (SBN) a terrorist organis.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Union home minister Amit Shah on Wednesday said the Centre has declared the Pakistan-based Shahzad Bhatti Network (SBN) a terrorist organisation under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA).He said the decision was taken in keeping with Prime Minister Narendra Modi's vision of adopting a zero-tolerance approach towards terrorism."The group is involved in smuggling of arms, explosives and narcotics across borders, apart from inciting youths and petty criminals into terrorism. Targeting India's democratic structure and the fabric of communal harmony, the syndicate also published hateful digital content," Shah said in a post on X.A gazette notification issued by the Union Home Ministry on Wednesday invoked Section 35(1)(a) of the UAPA to add "Shahzad Bhatti Network (SBN)" to the First Schedule of the Act, which lists organisations designated as terrorist groups.The Centre said the action was taken based on its assessment that SBN was involved in "terrorism and has participated in various acts of terrorism in India.""'Shahzad Bhatti Network (SBN)' is an organisation whose objective is to involve gullible youth and local criminals to smuggle arms, explosives, and narcotics from across the border, and through terrorist activities, pose a serious threat to the democratic system, communal harmony, and internal security of the country," the notification said.The notification cited criminal cases registered against alleged SBN members under laws including the UAPA, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Arms Act, Explosives Act, Information Technology Act and Prevention of Defacement of Property Act.The notification cited criminal cases against alleged SBN members under laws including the UAPA, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Arms Act, Explosives Act, Information Technology Act and Prevention of Defacement of Property Act.It said the SBN was involved in "radicalising gullible youth" through various allurements, motivating them to engage in anti-national activities and mobilising resources for such acts in collusion with other banned outfits and similarly designated entities."And whereas, the 'Shahzad Bhatti Network (SBN)' is promoting terrorism through violent activities that disrupt public order and by using various digital communication platforms to disseminate provocative messages, posing a serious challenge to the integrity of the nation," the notification read.The move comes nearly a month after a coordinated operation was carried out across 14 states to disrupt the SBN terror network and thwart its plans for subversive attacks ahead of Independence Day. The operation resulted in 253 detentions and more than 200 arrests, with over 80 FIRs registered against alleged SBN operatives.The ministry of home affairs (MHA) said on August 12 that the multi-state operation was conducted in coordination with state police forces using a real-time intelligence-sharing system. The 253 detentions included 62 in Uttar Pradesh, 52 in Haryana, 51 in Delhi, 44 in Punjab, 15 in Rajasthan, eight in Maharashtra, five in Uttarakhand, three each in Karnataka, Gujarat and Bihar, and two each in Telangana, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir and Kerala. Fresh FIRs were registered in Delhi and Karnataka.According to the MHA, SBN, described as a Pakistan-based ISI-backed terror syndicate, is linked to grenade, IED and petrol bomb attacks and targeted killings across India. The group has also been accused of paying local conduits to conduct reconnaissance of police, defence and religious sites and install CCTV cameras for espionage.Under the UAPA, inclusion in the First Schedule formally designates an organisation as "terrorist" under Indian law. With the latest addition, SBN becomes the 46th organisation on the list.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: EU opens door for Canada amid trade war with Trump, proposes first-ever associate membership
articles.summary: Europe News: In a major bid to deepen ties with Ottawa amid growing trade tensions with Washington, European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday.
articles.body: In a major bid to deepen ties with Ottawa amid growing trade tensions with Washington, European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday invited Canada to become the European Union’s first associate member.She proposed a new partnership spanning trade, defence, technology, energy and critical minerals.“I invite Canada to be the first associate member of the EU,” von der Leyen said on Wednesday during her annual State of the European Union address at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, according to ANI.Canadian prime minister Mark Carney, who was seated in the front row, responded by embracing von der Leyen as lawmakers applauded. He is due to address the European parliament on Thursday.Von der Leyen said Brussels wanted to take the relationship beyond the existing Canada-EU trade agreement, the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA).“We will move from CETA to an Alliance for the Future. To create a common prosperity and economic security space,” she said.The proposed arrangement would cover areas including advanced manufacturing, technology, defence production, energy, critical minerals, batteries, artificial intelligence, quantum technologies, cybersecurity and the Arctic.“This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” von der Leyen said. “In short, we want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible.”She also pointed to what she described as shared democratic principles between Canada and the 27-member bloc.“Above all, dear Mark, Europe and Canada believe in democracy,” von der Leyen said. “We believe that power does not belong to the strongest, the richest or the loudest, but to all of us. That democracies have the freedom to choose with whom to work.”The proposal would not amount to full EU membership. The bloc’s treaties restrict full membership to European states, making an associate-member arrangement a possible new model for closer cooperation with a non-European country.A Canadian official familiar with the discussions previously told The Associated Press that Ottawa was examining an arrangement that could include closer mobility between Canada and Europe, including possible visa-free rights to live and work in EU countries.Carney’s office backed the push for closer ties, saying Canada was working with the EU “to strengthen our sovereignty”. Ottawa has also supported expanding the relationship beyond CETA.The initiative comes as Canada seeks to diversify its economic partnerships. Around 70 per cent of Canadian exports go to the US, leaving the country particularly exposed to changes in Washington’s trade policy.Carney has argued that middle powers need to strengthen cooperation rather than negotiate separately with dominant economies.“When we only negotiate bilaterally with a hegemon, we negotiate from weakness. We accept what is offered,” Carney said at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January.“This is not sovereignty,” he added. “It is the performance of sovereignty while accepting subordination.”Canada has already become the first non-European country to join the EU’s €150 billion SAFE defence procurement programme, giving Canadian companies access to joint purchasing arrangements.The details of the proposed associate membership remain unclear.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The government has ruled out any rollback of the proposed 0.4 per cent Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on Unified Payments Interface (UPI) tra.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The government has ruled out any rollback of the proposed 0.4 per cent Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions above Rs 2,000, saying the decision has already been taken and will come into effect from October 15.“There is no question of a re-think,” a top government official told news agency PTI when asked whether the Centre was considering withdrawing the proposed MDR on high-value merchant transactions.The decision comes amid sharp criticism from Opposition parties, traders and sections of the digital payments ecosystem who dubbed the move as 'Modi Tax'. Congress leader Rahul Gandhi accusing Prime Minister Narendra Modi of yielding to US pressure over the new UPI framework, .Earlier in the day, in a video posted on X on Wednesday, Gandhi attacked Modi over the revised UPI framework, alleging that the Prime Minister had taken a different approach.“Modiji has a completely diff concept, he's neither left or right he has decided to completely lie down straight and in front of Donald Trump. He's put a tax on every single Indian person by taxing UPI and giving huge amount op money to the United States,” the former Congress president added.Also read: New UPI charges challenged in SC; petitioner flags impact on common manGandhi later said: “Modiji, please stop lying down in front of the US. Have a spine, stand up and withdraw the UPI tax. Thank you."The Centre has rejected the allegation that the changes were driven by foreign pressure. The finance ministry said on Wednesday that India’s UPI policy decisions were being taken independently with the objective of creating a sustainable and inclusive digital payments ecosystem.“Debunking the ‘External Pressure’ Myth: Some claims suggest the change is due to foreign influence. This is false. India’s UPI policy decisions are made independently, with the clear goal of building a self-sustaining, inclusive, and affordable digital payments ecosystem,” the ministry stated on X.Government sources cited by PTI said the MDR framework was aimed at strengthening the UPI ecosystem, including its safety and security, while making the system financially sustainable.The finance ministry has also stressed that customers will not be charged for UPI payments. “MDR is a charge within the merchant payment ecosystem. It is not a charge on customers making UPI payments,” it said.Person-to-person transfers will remain free, while merchants receiving up to Rs 1 lakh a month through QR codes will continue to have zero-MDR protection, according to the ministry. It said more than 95 per cent of merchant payments are below Rs 2,000.The move follows concerns raised by Parliament’s Standing Committee on Finance in its 32nd report, over the financial sustainability of the zero-MDR regime. The panel had noted that the government was spending roughly Rs 2,000 crore annually to support the incentive scheme.With the new framework set to take effect on October 15, the government is now expected to focus on implementation, merchant incentives and the expansion of UPI in rural and semi-urban areas.Get the latest India News and Live updates. and narcotics smuggling over the years.He has also been linked to the killing of Punjabi singer Sidhu Moose Wala in 2022, according to sources, news agency PTI reported.The government on Wednesday said.He was also allegedly involved in the 2024 murder of NCP leader Baba Siddique, with sources saying he assisted Zeeshan Akhtar, a key conspirator in the case, in fleeing India and settling in articles.title: 150-million-year-old giant long-necked dinosaur fossils found in Spain mark the first evidence beyond North America
articles.summary: Europe News: Spanish palaeontologists have identified fossils of ‘Diplodocus’ in Teruel, which marks the first evidence of the iconic long-necked dinosaur outside .
articles.body: Spanish palaeontologists have identified fossils of ‘Diplodocus’ in Teruel, which marks the first evidence of the iconic long-necked dinosaur outside North America. The remains were recovered from the La Tejería site in El Castellar and date to about 150 million years ago. The material includes 14 well-preserved tail vertebrae and several chevron bones. According to research published in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology, researchers identified the specimen as Diplodocus after examining its anatomy and comparing it with other diplodocine sauropods, alongside evolutionary analyses. The study places the animal within the Diplodocus genus and notes that giant sauropods could have moved between North America and Europe during the Late Jurassic.Where did researchers find the 150-million-year-old long-necked dinosaur fossilsResearchers identified the dinosaur remains at the La Tejería fossil site in El Castellar, Teruel, Spain. The material consists of 14 preserved caudal vertebrae and several chevron bones from the tail. According to the Spanish paleontological research institution, the fossils date to approximately 150 million years ago, placing them near the end of the Jurassic Period. Anatomical study revealed features associated with Diplodocus, including large pneumatic cavities in the vertebrae, deep longitudinal grooves along the underside of tail bones, forked chevrons with distinctive medial fossae, and elongated vertebral centra without lateral ridges. These characteristics, together with evolutionary analyses, allowed the researchers to place the specimen within Diplodocus.How were the Teruel fossils identified as ‘Diplodocus’The identification was based on anatomical comparisons and phylogenetic analyses. Researchers examined tail vertebrae and chevron bones and compared their structures with those of diplodocine sauropods. Its vertebrae contained large pneumatic cavities and deep grooves on their underside, while the chevron bones were forked and contained distinctive medial fossae. The vertebral centra were elongated and lacked lateral ridges. The team used analyses, including maximum parsimony and Bayesian inference, to test the anatomical evidence. These analyses placed the specimen within the Diplodocus genus.What makes the Teruel Diplodocus significant among giant sauropodsThe El Castellar Diplodocus was estimated to have reached about 25 metres in length, placing it among the giant sauropods known from the Spanish Jurassic. Its size was comparable to that of North American relatives. The researchers noted that other giant sauropods from the region, including Turiasaurus and Losillasaurus, had characteristics that were different from diplodocids. The fossils therefore add to sauropod diversity in Jurassic Spain. Their preservation also revealed anatomical details that are important for identification.What does Diplodocus reveal about dinosaur movement between continentsThe discovery also offers clues about how dinosaurs moved between continents during the Late Jurassic. The researchers interpret the Spanish Diplodocus as evidence of faunal exchange between North America and Europe at a time when the proto-Atlantic Ocean was still developing. They suggest that temporary land connections may have formed during periods when sea levels fell across the proto-North Atlantic.These connections could have allowed terrestrial animals to move between the two landmasses. The presence of Diplodocus in Iberia supports the possibility of intercontinental dispersal across the emerging Atlantic and provides new evidence for understanding how changing geography shaped dinosaur distributions during the Late Jurassic.What does the Teruel fossil reveal about Diplodocus in EuropeThe Diplodocus fossils provide new evidence of sauropod diversity in eastern Iberia. Teruel has produced fossils representing dinosaur groups, including sauropods, theropods, stegosaurs and ornithopods. The study shows their value for understanding Mesozoic ecosystems and European sauropod diversity. The fossils provide the first evidence of the Diplodocus genus outside North America. The researchers place the specimen close to Diplodocus hallorum, although the available material does not establish a particular species. The fossils are currently preserved and displayed at Dinópolis in Teruel.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: A New Jersey lawyer began diving for shipwrecks with her partner; after his death in 2025, she continued searching for lost treasures
articles.summary: US News: Jennifer Sellitti is a New Jersey public defender by day and a shipwreck diver by choice. For more than a decade, she explored the North Atlantic's su.
articles.body: Jennifer Sellitti is a New Jersey public defender by day and a shipwreck diver by choice. For more than a decade, she explored the North Atlantic's sunken vessels alongside her partner, Joe Mazraani, aboard their boat, D/V Tenacious, helping locate several long-lost wrecks off the Eastern Seaboard. After Mazraani died during a deep-sea dive in 2025, Sellitti took command of their company, Atlantic Wreck Salvage, continuing the dangerous search for lost ships that the two of them once shared.From the courtroom to deep sea: Jennifer Sellitti's path into shipwreck divingSellitti graduated from Boston University in 1996 and built a career as a criminal defence attorney and public defender in New Jersey. She had never gone diving until she met Joe Mazraani in 2015, a fellow criminal defence lawyer who had been wreck diving off the Northeast coast since the mid-1990s. Mazraani, who was born in Lebanon and immigrated to the United States at 15, introduced her to his obsession with the roughly 5,400 shipwrecks resting on the Atlantic's floor. Sellitti quickly took to the sport, training as a diver and eventually earning a US Coast Guard captain's license alongside her legal career.Jennifer Sellitti's shipwreck discoveries aboard D/V TenaciousAs stated in the archives of The Atlantic Wreck Salvage, Sellitti and Mazraani co-captained D/V Tenacious, a former fishing boat Mazraani had repurposed for deep-sea salvage after founding Atlantic Wreck Salvage in 2010. Together they led crews to several previously undocumented wrecks, including the WWI troopship SS West Point and the bow of the MV Stockholm, the ship that collided with the SS Andrea Doria off Nantucket in 1956. In 2016, Sellitti took on her own project, searching for Le Lyonnais, a French passenger steamship that sank in 1856. The wreck was finally located by the Tenacious team in 2024, a discovery she later chronicled in her book, The Adriatic Affair.The dive that took Jennifer Sellitti's partner, Joe MazraaniAccording to The Guardian, on July 29, 2025, Mazraani suffered a medical emergency while diving to an unidentified wreck the team called the "Big Engine Steamer," roughly 200 miles off the Massachusetts coast on Georges Bank. Sellitti was aboard Tenacious that day. The crew brought him back to the boat and attempted CPR, but could not revive him. Speaking on behalf of Atlantic Wreck Salvage, Sellitti said there was no reason to suspect diver error or equipment failure, and that a full investigation was underway. She has said she still finds it difficult to discuss the loss of the man who introduced her to shipwreck diving.Jennifer Sellitti now leads Atlantic Wreck Salvage and D/V TenaciousSince Mazraani's death, Sellitti has taken the helm of Atlantic Wreck Salvage and D/V Tenacious, continuing the expeditions they once ran together. As Managing Member, she leads dives, conducts historical research, oversees side-scan sonar surveys, and works to educate the public about shipwreck discovery and responsible salvage. She is an associate member of the Boston Sea Rovers and a trustee of the New Jersey Maritime Museum. When she is not at sea, she works as a criminal defence attorney. Her first book, The Adriatic Affair: A Maritime Hit-And-Run Off the Coast of Nantucket, tells the story of the sinking of the Nineteenth-century passenger steamship, Le Lyonnais. “All I know is,” she told The Guardian while remembering Joe, “that the further from shore I am, the closer I am to him.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
